title: The relative pronoun

objectives.can: Parse a relative pronoun and find its antecedent: gender and number from the antecedent, case from its own clause.

explanation.summary: A relative pronoun joins a clause to a noun it describes: 'the field which Jacob gave', 'the man who came'. The Greek relative ὅς ἥ ὅ takes its gender and number from that noun, but its case from the job it does inside its own clause.

sections.heading: What a relative pronoun does
body: A relative pronoun starts a relative clause. It points back to a word in the main clause, called the antecedent ('the one that goes before'), and it also does a job inside its own clause, as subject, object, possessor and so on.

In John 4:5 the relative is ὃ: 'the plot of land which Jacob gave to his son Joseph'. The antecedent is χωρίου, the plot of land. Inside the relative clause, ὃ is what Jacob gave, so it is the direct object of ἔδωκεν.

sections.heading: Two rules: agreement and case
body: Gender and number come from the antecedent. Case comes from the relative's own clause. That is the whole grammar of the pronoun, and it is the habit you must acquire: look back for the antecedent to fix gender and number; look at the relative clause to fix the case.

In John 4:12 the antecedent is Ἰακώβ, genitive because it depends on τοῦ πατρός. But the relative that follows is ὃς, nominative, because Jacob is the one who did the giving: he is the subject of ἔδωκεν. Gender (masculine) and number (singular) agree with Jacob; the case does not.

sections.heading: The forms: the article without τ
body: Most forms of ὅς look like the article with the initial τ replaced by a rough breathing and with an accent: the article's τοῦ, τῷ, τόν, τήν, τῶν, τοῖς correspond to the relative's οὗ, ᾧ, ὅν, ἥν, ὧν, οἷς. The differences from the article are few. The masculine nominative singular is ὅς, where the article has ὁ. The relative always carries an accent, which is how you tell the nominative plurals οἵ and αἵ from the article's unaccented οἱ and αἱ.

The neuter nominative and accusative singular is ὅ, and the plural is ἅ, as in the article. The charts below are filled from forms that occur in the New Testament; a dash means that form does not occur there.

sections.heading: ὅστις and ὅσος
body: ὅστις is ὅς joined to the indefinite τις. Both halves can decline, but in the New Testament nearly every form you meet is nominative: ὅστις, ἥτις, οἵτινες, αἵτινες. It often describes the kind of person or thing, or the whole class: 'anyone who', 'one who is of the sort that'. In 1 John 1:2 ἥτις takes its feminine singular from τὴν ζωὴν and is the subject of ἦν.

ὅσος is the relative of quantity: 'as much as', 'as many as'. Its forms are those of an ordinary adjective of the first and second declensions. In John 1:12 ὅσοι begins the clause with no noun to point back to.

sections.heading: When the antecedent is missing, or changes case
body: Greek often leaves the antecedent out when it is obvious or general. Then the relative clause itself works as a noun: 'the one who', 'whoever', 'the thing which', 'all who'. The relative still takes its case from its own clause. In John 1:12, ὅσοι gives the sense 'all who', 'as many as', and the clause is the subject of ἔδωκεν.

Sometimes the relative is drawn into the case of its antecedent. This is called attraction. In John 4:14, the water Jesus will give is the object of δώσω, so you would expect the accusative ὃ, and later in the same verse that is just what you find. But the first relative is οὗ, the genitive, matching the genitive ὕδατος before it. Luke 5:9 has the same thing with ὧν after τῶν ἰχθύων. Attraction is most often seen when the antecedent is genitive or dative; when a relative is in a case that its clause does not seem to need, look at the antecedent.

misunderstandings: Taking the relative's case from its antecedent. In ὃς ἔδωκεν, 'who gave', the relative is nominative as the subject of the verb, whatever case the antecedent is in.
Reading the accented relative οἵ or αἵ as the article οἱ or αἱ. The article has no accent and begins a noun phrase; the relative begins a clause with its own verb.
Treating ὅ as the article. The article has the forms ὁ and τό; ὅ is the neuter relative and carries an accent.
Assuming an English relative word ('who', 'which', 'that') always fixes the Greek: the Greek form is chosen by the antecedent's gender and number, not by whether English would say 'who' or 'which'.

deeper.heading: Relative and demonstrative
body: ὅς, ἥ, ὅ is historically related to the article, and in older Greek it was a demonstrative too. In the New Testament the relative use is overwhelmingly the normal one. Relative clauses with an indefinite sense, such as the one beginning ὃς δ’ ἂν πίῃ in John 4:14, are a construction of their own; for now it is enough to read that clause as 'whoever drinks'.

Because the relative is always genitive after a plural noun
Because the sentence has no antecedent

options: As a vocative address to a group
